title: The Broken Covenant
overview: Jeremiah 11 reveals God's solemn reminder to Judah and Jerusalem about the covenant made with their ancestors, emphasizing obedience as the condition for blessing. The chapter highlights Israel’s persistent rebellion, idolatry, and the resulting judgment that God will bring upon them. Jeremiah is commissioned to proclaim this message publicly, warning of the consequences of forsaking God’s commands. The chapter also exposes a conspiracy against Jeremiah, illustrating the personal cost of prophetic obedience. This passage underscores the seriousness of covenant faithfulness and God’s righteous judgment, setting the tone for much of Jeremiah’s ministry and the impending exile.
structure:
**Verses 1-5: The Covenant Reminder.** God commands Jeremiah to remind the people of Judah and Jerusalem about the covenant made at the Exodus, emphasizing obedience as the key to being God's people and receiving His promised blessings.

**Verses 6-8: The Call to Proclaim and the People's Disobedience.** Jeremiah is instructed to proclaim the covenant publicly, but the people continue to reject God's voice and follow their own evil imaginations.

**Verses 9-14: The Conspiracy and Judgment Pronounced.** God reveals a conspiracy among the people who have returned to idolatry, breaking the covenant. Judgment is declared, including the futility of their prayers and reliance on false gods.

**Verses 15-17: The Lord’s Grief and Judgment.** God laments Israel’s unfaithfulness, describing them as a once flourishing olive tree now broken by judgment because of their idolatry.

**Verses 18-23: Jeremiah’s Persecution and Divine Protection.** Jeremiah reveals knowledge of a plot against his life by men of Anathoth, but God promises to punish his enemies and protect His prophet.

keyVerses.text: And say thou unto them, Thus saith the LORD God of Israel; Cursed be the man that obeyeth not the words of this covenant,
keyVerses.significance: This verse establishes the covenantal framework and the serious consequences of disobedience, highlighting the conditional nature of Israel’s relationship with God.

keyVerses.text: Yet they obeyed not, nor inclined their ear, but walked every one in the imagination of their evil heart: therefore I will bring upon them all the words of this covenant, which I commanded them to do; but they did them not.
keyVerses.significance: It underscores the persistent rebellion of the people despite God’s repeated warnings, justifying the judgment that follows.

keyVerses.text: Therefore thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will bring evil upon them, which they shall not be able to escape; and though they shall cry unto me, I will not hearken unto them.
keyVerses.significance: This verse reveals the irrevocable judgment due to covenant breach, emphasizing God’s righteous justice and the consequences of persistent disobedience.

keyVerses.text: The LORD called thy name, A green olive tree, fair, and of goodly fruit: with the noise of a great tumult he hath kindled fire upon it, and the branches of it are broken.
keyVerses.significance: This metaphor illustrates Israel’s former blessing and current devastation, symbolizing the loss of God’s favor due to their sin.

keyVerses.text: Therefore thus saith the LORD of the men of Anathoth, that seek thy life, saying, Prophesy not in the name of the LORD, that thou die not by our hand:
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights the opposition Jeremiah faces for faithfully proclaiming God’s word, showing the cost of prophetic obedience.

characters.name: Jeremiah
characters.description: The prophet called by God to deliver a message of covenant warning and judgment to Judah and Jerusalem. He faithfully proclaims God’s word despite opposition and threats to his life.

characters.name: The LORD (God)
characters.description: The sovereign covenant-maker who reminds His people of their obligations, pronounces judgment for disobedience, and protects His prophet Jeremiah.

characters.name: Men of Anathoth
characters.description: A group conspiring against Jeremiah, seeking to silence him by threatening his life because of his prophetic messages.

themes.description: The chapter centers on the covenant between God and Israel, emphasizing obedience as essential for blessing and disobedience as deserving judgment, reflecting the biblical theme of covenant loyalty.
Israel’s return to idolatry and rejection of God’s commands provoke divine judgment, illustrating the biblical principle that worship of false gods leads to ruin.
Jeremiah’s experience of threats and conspiracies against his life highlights the cost of faithful prophetic ministry in a rebellious nation.
While God pronounces judgment for covenant breach, He also reveals His knowledge and control over events, promising justice against the conspirators and protection for His servant.

historicalContext: Jeremiah prophesied during the late 7th and early 6th centuries BC, a time of political instability in Judah under threat from Babylonian expansion. The people had repeatedly broken the Mosaic covenant by worshiping Baal and other gods, reflecting widespread syncretism. The covenant was central to Israel’s identity, rooted in the Exodus event when God delivered them from Egypt. Jeremiah’s ministry occurred in Jerusalem, the religious and political heart of Judah, where idolatry and political conspiracies flourished. The men of Anathoth, Jeremiah’s hometown, opposed him, reflecting internal divisions and resistance to prophetic warnings.

theologicalInterpretations.description: This interpretation emphasizes God’s sovereign covenant and the necessity of obedience. Jeremiah’s warnings are seen as a call to repentance, with judgment as a just consequence of covenant breach, highlighting God’s holiness and justice.

Dispensationalists view this chapter as part of Israel’s national covenant history, with the judgment pronounced as a temporal consequence leading to exile. They often see Jeremiah’s message as distinct from the church age, focusing on Israel’s future restoration.

Early church interpreters often saw Jeremiah’s covenant warnings typologically, viewing Israel’s disobedience as a foreshadowing of humanity’s fall and the need for Christ’s redemptive covenant, with Jeremiah as a type of the suffering prophet.

crossReferences.connection: God’s covenant with Israel at Sinai, emphasizing obedience and the promise to make Israel His treasured people, parallels Jeremiah’s covenant reminder.
The curses for covenant disobedience outlined here are echoed in Jeremiah’s pronouncement of judgment for breaking the covenant.
The contrast between the blessed man who delights in God’s law and the wicked who perish aligns with Jeremiah’s call for covenant obedience.
Isaiah’s indictment of Judah’s rebellion and idolatry complements Jeremiah’s message of covenant breach and judgment.
Jesus’ lament over Jerusalem’s rejection of God’s prophets echoes Jeremiah’s depiction of Israel’s persistent disobedience and impending judgment.

application: Regularly examine your life for covenant faithfulness by aligning your actions with God’s Word.
Respond promptly and obediently to God’s commands to avoid the consequences of disobedience.
Trust God’s justice when facing opposition or persecution for your faith, knowing He sees and will act.
Avoid idolatry in all forms by keeping God central in your worship and daily life.
Pray earnestly for your community but recognize that God’s hearing depends on genuine repentance and obedience.
conclusion: Jeremiah 11 powerfully reminds believers of the seriousness of God’s covenant and the dire consequences of unfaithfulness. It calls for heartfelt obedience and warns against the dangers of idolatry and rebellion. The chapter also reveals the personal cost of faithful witness through Jeremiah’s persecution, encouraging believers to trust God’s justice and protection. Its timeless message challenges Christians today to remain steadfast in covenant loyalty, embrace God’s Word fully, and rely on His grace amid trials.
timeline: c. 627-605 BC - Jeremiah’s early prophetic ministry during the reign of King Josiah and the rise of Babylonian power

outline.heading: The Covenant Command
outline.description: God instructs Jeremiah to remind Judah and Jerusalem of the covenant made at the Exodus, emphasizing obedience as the condition for blessing.

outline.heading: Proclamation and Rejection
outline.description: Jeremiah is commanded to proclaim the covenant publicly, but the people persist in disobedience and evil imaginations.

outline.heading: Conspiracy and Judgment Declared
outline.description: God reveals a conspiracy among the people who have returned to idolatry, pronounces inevitable judgment, and forbids Jeremiah from praying on their behalf.

outline.heading: The Lord’s Lament and Judgment
outline.description: God mourns Israel’s unfaithfulness, symbolized by a broken olive tree, and declares judgment for their idolatry.

outline.heading: Jeremiah’s Persecution and Divine Justice
outline.description: Jeremiah reveals knowledge of a plot against his life, prays for God’s justice, and God promises punishment for his enemies.
